title: Bubble Sort
explanation:
**Bubble sort** is the simplest sorting algorithm to understand (though not to use in practice). It repeatedly walks the list comparing **adjacent** pairs and swapping any that are out of order. After each full pass, the largest remaining element has "bubbled" to its correct place at the end — so each pass can stop one element earlier.

It is a great teaching example precisely because its cost is easy to see: two nested loops, each roughly proportional to n, give **O(n²)** comparisons. For an already-sorted list it still does O(n²) comparisons in this basic form (an optimized version adds an early-exit flag to make the best case O(n)). It uses **O(1)** extra space and is **stable** (equal elements keep their order).

In real code you would call Python's built-in `sorted` (O(n log n)). Bubble sort earns its place as the clearest illustration of the nested-loop → quadratic relationship, which the complexity panel's comparison counter makes concrete.

vocabulary.definition: Repeatedly swapping adjacent out-of-order elements until sorted.
One sweep through the list; after pass i, the largest i elements are in place.
Equal elements keep their original relative order.
Sorts using O(1) extra space (here, ignoring the defensive copy).

concepts.purpose: Teach the mechanics of sorting and the nested-loop → O(n²) relationship.
concepts.operations: Compare adjacent pairs; swap if out of order; shrink the range each pass.
concepts.uses: Educational; tiny inputs; not for production (use sorted / Timsort).
concepts.tradeoffs: O(n²) time, O(1) space, stable — simple but slow; beaten by O(n log n) sorts.
concepts.commonMistakes: Looping the inner range to n (not n-1-i) causing index errors; claiming O(n) without the early-exit optimization; forgetting stability.
concepts.edgeCases: Empty/one-element list is already sorted. Already-sorted input still O(n²) in the basic form.

complexity.note: Basic form; early-exit variant is O(n) best case.

variables.meaning: the number of elements in the list

complexityExplanation.costModel: Each adjacent comparison and swap is O(1). The nested loops determine the comparison count.

time.explanation: The outer loop runs n times; the inner loop runs about n-1, n-2, … comparisons across passes. Summed, that is (n-1)+(n-2)+…+1 = n(n-1)/2 comparisons — O(n²). Because the loops are NESTED, the counts multiply into a quadratic. The basic form does this many comparisons even on sorted input.

otherCases.note: With an early-exit flag that stops when a pass makes no swaps (e.g. already sorted).

space.explanation: Sorting happens by swapping within the list; only loop indices are extra. (The defensive a[:] copy is O(n) but is for safety, not the algorithm's working space.)
space.inputOutputNote: The a[:] copy of n elements is made so the input isn't mutated; the sort itself is in place.

derivation.description: The outer loop runs n times.
The inner loop does up to n-1-i comparisons per pass; nested → about n²/2 total.
Only the copy grows with n; the sort itself uses O(1) working space.

assumptions: This is the basic form without the early-exit optimization.
complexityExplanation.tradeoffs: O(n log n) sorts (merge/quick/Timsort) are dramatically faster for large n; bubble sort is only competitive on tiny or nearly-sorted inputs (with early exit).
complexityExplanation.fixedDataNote: This run sorts 5 elements, doing 4+3+2+1 = 10 comparisons. The O(n²) bound generalises that triangular count to n.

codeExplanations.explanation: Copy the input so the caller's list is not mutated.
Outer loop: one pass per element (n passes).
Inner loop: compare up to n-1-i pairs (the last i are already sorted).
If a pair is out of order...
...swap them. Large values bubble toward the end.

prediction.prompt: How many comparisons does basic bubble sort do on 5 elements, and what is the general formula?
prediction.explanation: The passes do 4+3+2+1 = 10 comparisons for n=5. In general the sum is n(n-1)/2, which is quadratic.

exercises.prompt: `bubble_sort(a)` should sort the list in place and return it, but the inner range reads past the end and raises an index error. Fix the inner range.
hints: Goal: fix the inner loop range so bubble sort does not index out of bounds.
The comparison reads a[j+1], which runs past the end when j reaches the last index.
Key insight: after i passes, the last i elements are already in place and need no comparison.
Approach: shrink the inner range each pass to stop before the sorted tail.
Pseudocode: for i in range(n): for j in range(n - 1 - i): if a[j] > a[j+1]: swap.
Use `range(n - 1 - i)` for the inner loop so a[j+1] stays in bounds.
exercises.tests:
assert bubble_sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8]) == [1, 2, 4, 5, 8], 'sorts a mixed list'
assert bubble_sort([]) == [], 'empty list'
assert bubble_sort([1]) == [1], 'single element'
assert bubble_sort([3, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 3], 'reversed input'
assert bubble_sort([2, 2, 1]) == [1, 2, 2], 'duplicates'
print('OK')

exercises.prompt: For n = 1,000,000 elements, is bubble sort acceptable? What should you use and why?
exercises.expected: No — O(n²) would be ~10^12 operations. Use an O(n log n) sort (Python's sorted/Timsort), which is ~2×10^7 operations.
hints: Goal: decide whether bubble sort is acceptable for n = 1,000,000 elements, and if not, what to use.
The costly reality is bubble sort's O(n²): for a million elements that is about 10^12 operations.
Key property: n is large enough that the quadratic-versus-log-linear gap is the difference between seconds and hours.
Approach: use an O(n log n) comparison sort such as Python's built-in sorted (Timsort).
Reasoning: O(n log n) is roughly 2×10^7 operations here, tens of thousands of times fewer than O(n²); bubble sort is only tolerable for tiny or nearly-sorted inputs.
Answer: no — O(n²) is ~10^12 ops; use an O(n log n) sort (sorted/Timsort), ~2×10^7 ops.

review: **Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, bubbling the largest to the end each pass. Its **nested loops** make it **O(n²)** time (best O(n) only with an early-exit flag), **O(1)** space, and **stable**. It is a teaching tool for the nested-loop → quadratic relationship; use `sorted` (O(n log n)) in practice.
